text: Last lesson drew the line between security and privacy. Privacy rules exist to protect a specific category of data: PII, personally identifiable information. Let's define it precisely.

PII is information that can identify a specific person. The obvious cases are direct identifiers — a full name, a Social Security number, a passport number, an email address. Each one points at exactly one person on its own, and these are the fields every privacy review flags first.

Quasi-identifiers are more dangerous precisely because they look harmless. A ZIP code alone doesn't identify you. A birth date alone doesn't either. But Latanya Sweeney's landmark research found that just three fields together — five-digit ZIP code, full birth date, and gender — uniquely identify a large majority of the US population. Strip the name and you can still re-identify most people.

PII is a US-centric term, and it's narrower than it sounds. GDPR uses a broader concept: personal data — any information relating to an identified or identifiable person. That catches things PII often doesn't: an IP address, a device ID, a cookie, location history. Under GDPR, 'is this PII' is the wrong question.

Next lesson draws a sharper line still: sensitive data, which can harm a person if exposed, versus confidential data, which an organization protects for business reasons — two overlapping but distinct categories that set up how Chapter 2's classification labels actually work.
